newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thailand sees gains for tourism from baht float.
newsitem.headline: Thailand sees gains for tourism from baht float.

text.p: The state-run Tourism Authority of Thailand (TAT) on Wednesday welcomed the government's decision to float the baht, saying it would augur well for the tourism industry.

"We are positive that this decision will eventually help revitalise the country's overall economy, although there will be some difficulties and drawbacks along the way as we try to implement this policy," the TAT said in a statement.
The Thai government on July 2 changed the exchange rate system to a managed float from a 13-year old policy of pegging the baht to a basket of currencies dominated by U.S. dollar.
Visitors would get more baht per dollar and this would boost sales of local products.
"Shopping is the main source of income from Thai tourism. In 1996, tourists spent nearly 10.2 million baht ($351,724) per day on shopping, up from about 7.5 million baht per day in 1995," it said.
The floated baht would also make prices of local hotels cheaper in dollar terms.

"By prudently controlling their costs, especially those of the import contents, we believe that hotels, including tour operators, will also be able to enjoy more revenue as the flotation will increase our competitiveness in the market," the TAT said.
The authority said it expected about 7.8 million tourists in 1997, bringing in 240 billion baht in revenue, compared with 7.2 million tourists who spent about 219 billion baht in 1996.
